body:
[SIPHONED VERDICT]: Russia's diesel export ban — the first in its post-Soviet history — is a physical admission that Ukrainian drone strikes have structurally disrupted its fuel production. Russia is now importing fuel from a country it calls a brother nation while its own diesel goes up in smoke across an 1,800km arc from the Arctic to the Volga.

On July 9–10, Ukrainian drones struck oil facilities in Tver (Tver Oblast) and Vyazniki (Stavropol Krai), setting reservoirs ablaze. In the Sea of Azov, two more oil tankers were struck and set on fire, according to Rostov Governor Yuri Slyusar. These are the latest in a sustained Ukrainian drone campaign targeting Russian fuel infrastructure that began in late June.

Russia's government response was unprecedented: Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak, at a meeting chaired by Putin, announced an immediate ban on diesel exports. "This will allow us to increase supplies to the domestic market. In July, we will also begin importing petroleum products," Novak said. Russia — one of the world's top oil producers — is now importing fuel. Novak acknowledged that 20–25% of Russia's diesel production has been disrupted, with up to one-third of total refining capacity knocked offline at peak.

The Kremlin issued a statement acknowledging the strikes were causing fuel shortages. Kremlin spokesman Peskov said the strikes reflected "Washington's ambivalence" toward peace negotiations — acknowledging Ukrainian drone effectiveness without naming the specific campaign.

The Russian fuel crisis is now verifiable at the physical level. FIRMS (Firms.openearth.org) data shows thermal anomalies at oil depots across multiple Russian regions — Tver, Stavropol, Saratov, Astrakhan, Rostov — consistent with ongoing fires over multiple days. The regional rationing picture is documented across at least 15 Russian oblasts and territories, per Russian state media and local governors. Diesel prices on the Kola Peninsula reached 70–100 roubles/litre; Arkhangelsk hit 140 roubles/litre. Pinega district in Arkhangelsk has no gasoline at all. Murmansk has a 30-litre per-visit cap.

Russia's diesel export ban is verifiable — export customs data from July 10 onward should show zero diesel shipments, versus approximately 31 million tonnes per year that went to export before the strikes. Novak's statement is on the record acknowledging 20–25% production disruption and up to one-third of total refining capacity offline.

The tanker strikes in the Sea of Azov are separately verifiable via AIS data (Marine Traffic, Equasis) — the two vessels struck should show up as stationary or with last-position-reported in the Azov since July 9. Rostov governor named them; their AIS history would confirm whether they were shadow-fleet vessels, as prior Ukrainian Navy strikes have targeted.

The contradiction at the heart of this story: Russia launched the war to secure its sphere of influence and energy leverage. Ukrainian drones — increasingly long-range, hitting 800–1,500km deep — have turned that energy leverage inward. Putin banned diesel exports; Russia is now a fuel importer; domestic shortages span the Arctic to the Volga.

Novak's 20–25% production disruption figure, the Arctic rationing numbers (140 roubles/litre in Arkhangelsk, zero gasoline in Pinega, 30-litre caps in Murmansk), and the Sea of Azov tanker strikes together paint a complete picture of a fuel crisis that is structural, not temporary. Commercial SAR imagery (Sentinel-1, ICEYE) can confirm which specific facilities were struck. AIS data can confirm whether the Azov tankers were shadow-fleet vessels. The customs record of the export ban execution will show whether the ban holds or whether smuggling routes emerge.
narrative: Russia's diesel export ban is the physical evidence of failure that no amount of special military operation framing can hide. The FirMS thermal history across 8+ regions, the documented regional rationing statements from named governors, and Novak's on-record admission of 20–25% production disruption together tell a story Russia cannot spin.
analysis: The structural picture is stark: Russia launched this war in part to secure energy leverage over Europe. Ukrainian drones — firing from inside Ukraine at targets 800–1,500km deep inside Russia — have converted that leverage vector inward. The diesel ban means Russia does not have enough fuel for its own domestic market. That has never happened in Russia's post-Soviet export economy. The Sea of Azov tanker strikes add a maritime layer: Russia cannot protect its own coastal fuel transport from drone boats while simultaneously claiming to be winning a war whose stated rationale included energy security.
